idiom_name: separate Policy (decision) + Guard (enforcement point) + Rule model
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put every authorisation rule into one Policy component that answers a single question - may this subject perform this action on this resource? - from the security context, the request and the target's attributes. Wrap each protected operation in a Guard (a proxy, interceptor or wrapper) that collects those attributes, asks the Policy, denies by default and only then forwards the request to the resource; the resource itself contains no rule code. Express rules as (subject, action, resource) entries and keep the decision function pure so it can be tested without the resource, and keep the guard contract identical at every enforcement point so that no access path bypasses the policy.
code_sketch:
guard(action, resource):
    ctx = security_context(request)                  # subject, roles, attributes
    decision = policy.decide(ctx, action, resource)  # pure, deny by default
    if decision is DENY:
        audit(ctx, action, resource, decision)
        raise AccessDenied(decision.reason)
    return resource.perform(action)                  # rule-free resource code
pitfalls: An access path that reaches the resource without passing through a guard silently disables the policy (incomplete mediation).
Deciding from a stale or unverified security context - for example trusting client-supplied roles or claims - defeats the policy.
Caching decisions without invalidation keeps granting rights after they have been revoked (time-of-check versus time-of-use).
Wrong move: enforce authorization only in the browser or UI -> that fails because callers can forge requests and bypass presentation checks -> instead enforce the decision at every server-side Guard.

Wrong move: treat a policy-service timeout or indeterminate result as allow -> that fails open and turns an availability fault into privilege escalation -> instead deny, audit the failure, and retry only under an explicit bounded policy.

Wrong move: cache grants without policy-version, subject, and resource invalidation -> that fails by honoring revoked rights -> instead bind entries to a short expiry and invalidate them when policy or entitlements change.
